<document>
# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
I've read it closely and checked the numbers. Sections 1–5 do valuable work with data the original authors had and didn't use. Sections 6–8 then overreach in the opposite direction from Halden: having corrected an inflated claim, the comment ends up deflating what its own data still support.

## What the comment argues

- **Attrition (§1):** seven of the nine "preparation-phase" withdrawals actually left after the schedule began, mostly citing workload. The 61 are survivors.
- **Output measure (§2):** in the 23 organisations that submitted records, managers' indices exceeded the record-based index by 3.8 points on average, and in 19 of 23 cases.
- **Hours (§3):** in the 27 organisations with time tracking, actual hours fell 14.1%, not 20%. Combining records and actual hours (17 organisations), the per-hour gain is 10.8%, not 23.4%.
- **Revenue (§4):** +1.4% nominal is about −2.6% real.
- **Sectors (§5):** "gains in every sector" is guaranteed by how the per-hour figure is calculated, and retail output fell.
- **Novelty, meetings, conclusion (§6–8):** the residual 11% is plausibly novelty, the Varden meetings finding should not be cited, and per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty."

**Arithmetic check:**
- The Table 2 rows are all correct: 95.1/0.8 = +18.9%, 98.4/0.859 = +14.6%, 95.4/0.861 = +10.8%.
- The real-revenue figure is correct: 1.014/1.041 ≈ −2.6%.
- Two figures don't hold up; see points 2 and 5 below.

## What holds and should be stated plainly

- **The attrition finding is a real correction of the record.** The working paper's account of the withdrawals is contradicted by its own microdata. That should be fixed regardless of anything else.
- **The manager-reported index runs high.** A 19-of-23 split in one direction is good evidence of a systematic upward bias of about 4 points.
- **The scheduled-hours denominator overstates the reduction.** This independently confirms what the Varden trial found: 14% actual against 20% scheduled here, 13% against 20% there.
- **§4 and §5 are correct in substance.**
- **The corrected figure is roughly 11% in the subset where both corrections can be made**, subject to the subset caveat the authors themselves give.

## Issues within §1–4

**1. The abstract says three problems were corrected, but only two were.**
The abstract says "correcting the first three," and the first three include attrition. Table 2 corrects only output measurement and hours. Attrition is described but never quantified. A bound would fix this: recompute the mean output index assigning the nine withdrawals plausible values, such as the record-based retail mean or a worst case. With 9 of 70 organisations, the bound is probably a few points, which matters but isn't decisive.

**2. The hours components don't add up to the reported total.**
- Four days at 8 hours, plus 0.7 extra a day, plus 1.6 on the day off, gives about 36.4 hours. Starting from the baseline day of 40.3/5 gives about 36.7.
- The reported pilot average is 34.6.
- There may be an explanation, such as different denominators for day-off work, part-timers, or leave, but as written the components overshoot by roughly 2 hours.
- If the components are right and the total is wrong, the corrected gain is smaller still. If the total is right, the description of the components needs fixing.

**3. "Billable hours delivered" is partly an hours measure.**
For professional-services organisations whose records are billable hours, the record-based "output" falls mechanically with time worked. That biases the record-based index down for reasons that have nothing to do with manager optimism. It's worth reporting Table 1 with and without those organisations.

**4. CPI is a rough deflator, and there is still no comparison group.**
The real-terms point stands. "Revenue fell" still needs the caveat that revenue in non-participating firms may have moved too.

## Where the comment overreaches

**5. The novelty extrapolation is computed wrongly, and it's the wrong kind of evidence.**
- From +0.61 at month three to +0.29 at month six, a linear decline reaches zero at about month 8.7, not "around month ten."
- More importantly, two points don't establish a linear trend.
- The measure is self-reported energy, not output. Nothing in the data shows output per hour decaying.
- "Plausibly a novelty effect" is a reasonable hypothesis to carry forward as open. It doesn't justify "entirely an artifact."

**6. The comment cites one stratum of the Varden trial as decisive and ignores the other.**
§5 calls Varden's counter-stratum result "the most reliable finding in the literature." The case-processing stratum of the same trial has all of these features:
- it is randomised, with a control group, which addresses selection;
- it uses administrative output records, which addresses the output measure;
- it uses timesheet actual hours, which addresses the denominator;
- it runs to nine months, past the comment's own extrapolated zero point for novelty.

It found +12.5% per actual hour (CI +6.9 to +18.4). That is almost exactly the comment's corrected Halden figure, measured without the problems the comment identifies. The novelty critique doesn't straightforwardly apply either: control staff also knew a trial was under way, and the gain was measured at nine months. Varden's own caveats (claimed overtime only, few clusters) may shrink it, but they don't reduce it to zero. Using the trial's counter result while omitting its case-processing result is selective, and it is the most important problem in the comment.

**7. §7 mischaracterises the meetings analysis.**
- **Not post hoc:** the data were collected in month six at managers' request, before the nine-month results existed.
- **Not a subgroup:** the seven offices are the entire treated case-processing stratum.
- **The stronger evidence is a randomised comparison:** treated offices averaged 3.3 fewer hours of meetings than control offices (3.8 against 7.1 a week), measured at month six without a baseline. That is not a seven-point correlation.
- **The Varden authors already concluded this:** they said it "cannot establish a mechanism" and registered a confirmatory test.

The right status is an open hypothesis with a test pending, which is where Varden left it. Telling readers not to cite it shuts down a question that is already set up to be tested. And if the per-hour gain does come from removing low-value meeting time, that is a real gain in output per paid hour, not a measurement artifact.

**8. The conclusion contradicts the comment's own data note.**
The data note correctly says the corrected estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole." The abstract and conclusion then generalise beyond the pilot to "reduced-hours schemes" as a class. One uncontrolled pilot, even well corrected, can't support a claim about all schemes. And the strongest evidence on the subject, the Varden case-processing result, points the other way.

## Suggested revised conclusion

> Re-analysis of the Halden microdata shows that the reported 23.4% gain in output per hour is substantially overstated. Withdrawals were not random and occurred after the schedule began. Manager-reported output exceeded record-based output by about 4 points. Actual hours fell by about 14%, not 20%. In the 17 organisations where output and hours can both be measured directly, the implied gain is about 11%, before any adjustment for attrition, and this subset may not represent the pilot. That figure is close to the 12.5% found under randomisation in Varden County's case-processing offices. Whether such gains persist beyond nine months, and how much reflects reduced meeting time as against other mechanisms, remain open. In coverage-bound work, the randomised evidence shows reduced hours lower output per employee and worsen service.

This keeps every correction the comment earned and drops only the claims its data don't support.

If useful, I can write the attrition bound as a short worked calculation from the figures given. I could also draft a one-page synthesis of the three documents, showing where the Halden pilot, the Varden trial and this comment agree and what remains open.
